<meta>This page serves as the legal notice and copyright declaration for the work described on the previous page, "Memoirs on the Templars." It reflects the transition of French law during the Revolutionary period, moving from royal privileges to citizens' literary property rights.</meta>

### *Decree concerning Counterfeiters, issued on July 19, 1793, Year II of the Republic.*
<note>Year II refers to the second year of the French Revolutionary Calendar, which began in September 1792. This specific decree is a landmark in history, as it established the foundation for modern copyright law in France.</note>

Art. III. Peace Officers, Justices of the Peace, or Police Commissioners, shall be required to confiscate, at the request and for the benefit of Authors, Composers, Painters or Draftsmen and others, their Heirs or Assigns, all copies of printed or engraved editions published without the formal and written permission of the Authors.

Art. IV. Every Counterfeiter <note>In this context, "counterfeiter" refers to someone producing "pirated" or unauthorized copies of a book.</note> shall be required to pay the true Owner a sum equivalent to the price of three thousand copies of the original edition.

Art. V. Every Seller of a counterfeit edition, if not recognized as a Counterfeiter, shall be required to pay the true Owner a sum equivalent to the price of five hundred copies of the original edition.

---

I place the present edition under the safeguard of the Laws and the integrity of the Citizens. I declare that I will prosecute before the Courts any Counterfeiter, Distributor, or Seller of a counterfeit edition. I further promise to whoever identifies a Counterfeiter, Distributor, or Seller to me, half of the compensation granted by Law. The two copies, in accordance with the Law, have been deposited at the National Library.
<note>The requirement to deposit copies in a national library—known as "legal deposit"—ensures that a nation's published heritage is preserved and acts as proof of the publisher's claim to the work.</note>

This tragic adventure is recounted quite uniformly, in terms of its essential facts, by ancient historians <note>The author uses "anciens" to refer to medieval chroniclers and early historians who lived closer to the events than his own 19th-century audience.</note>. However, they differ as to its causes. They are divided into accusers and apologists of the Templars. The former constitute the majority. Only a few have chosen to believe them neither entirely guilty nor entirely innocent of the crimes that were imputed to them.

But the true spirit of events—which everything conspired to disguise from the eyes of contemporaries—is often better understood by a disinterested posterity. It would seem that modern authors should reach an agreement on this event, not only because the passage of time brings an end to all partiality, but because this same distance allows authentic records <term>monumens: In this historical context, the author uses "monuments" to refer to primary source documents, such as official trial records, papal bulls, and royal decrees, rather than stone structures.</term>,

### CHRONOLOGICAL SUMMARY

#### *Of the History of the Templars, and of their abolition.*

The exploits of the Templars fill every history of the Crusades; however, these histories also reveal the complaints voiced against them by both the Christian princes in the East and the crusading princes who came there to fight, as well as by the other religious orders who rivaled the Temple there. # OVERVIEW

## *Of the Constitution and Governance of the Order, as derived from the Rule, the Statutes, and the Trial Proceedings (1).*

---

### I. The Knights of the Temple.

To become a Knight of the Temple, one had to be descended from a family of knights, and born of a father who either was one or could have been one. It does not appear that there were, strictly speaking, formal "proofs of nobility" <note>Unlike later chivalric orders, the Templars initially relied on social standing and martial lineage rather than documented genealogical trees.</note>; one relied on the candidate's declaration: but severe punishments were imposed on anyone who lied; and, given the Order's extensive connections, the lie could not fail to be discovered.

It was necessary to be born of a legitimate marriage; an essential law for the Order's independence, where princes would have gladly placed their il- <note>The text likely completes as "illegitimate children" or "natural children" (enfants naturels), whom monarchs often sought to settle in wealthy religious orders to provide for them without dividing the royal inheritance.</note>

(1) This overview is largely drawn from a very extensive treatise that Professor Münter <note>Friedrich Münter (1761–1830), a scholar who published a significant German translation and analysis of the Templar Statutes.</note> included after his German translation of the Statutes.

<term>Templars</term> — Members of the military-religious Order of the Temple, founded in 1119.
<term>Rule</term> — The formal code of conduct for the Order, originally based on Cistercian principles.
<term>Statutes</term> — The "Retraits," or administrative regulations, which governed the Order's daily life and military operations.
<term>Trial Proceedings</term> — The official records of the depositions and interrogations conducted by the Inquisition and the French crown between 1307 and 1312.

<summary>This page begins a systematic overview of the Templars' internal regulations, specifically detailing the strict requirements for entry into the knighthood, such as knightly lineage and legitimate birth.</summary>

The candidate had to be free from any kind of bond or vow, being neither married, nor betrothed, nor committed to any other Order.

Finally, they required assurance that he was perfectly sound of body.

In the Rule, as in the statutes, there is no mention of a dowry to be paid by the candidate. However, it is certain that, in later times, this kind of simony <term>simony: the act of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices</term> was common. The new brother, under the name of a *subvention* <note>original: "subvention"; here meaning a mandatory "contribution" or "gift" to the Order upon entry</note>, purchased his admission with a sum of money or by the donation of property. The Order turned its admissions into a veritable trade. The proceedings of the papal commission <note>The judicial inquiry led by Pope Clement V during the trial of the Templars (1307–1312).</note> provide many proofs of this.

There was no fixed novitiate <term>novitiate: a probationary period for those entering a religious order</term>. The Master conducting the reception terminated or prolonged it as he saw fit; this was justified by the rule which required that the newly received member depart for Palestine without delay.

Moreover, since one could not be a Templar of the first class without having already received knighthood, the trials required for the latter implied that one was already prepared for the other rank.

The statutes say that children must not be received; but the records prove that many were admitted. The Church has always held dispensations <note>A dispensation is an exemption from a rule or law granted by an ecclesiastical authority.</note> alongside the laws.

To the three ordinary vows of obedience, chastity, and poverty, was added that of the defense of the Holy Land.

The habit of a Knight of the Temple was the white mantle, marked by a red cross. No priest, unless he were a bishop, and no serving brother, could wear this habit.

Each knight had a complete war equipage, with three horses, and a squire who was either a serving brother <term>serving brother: a member of the Order who was not a knight, responsible for various manual and military support tasks</term> or a salaried layman; sometimes it was a page or valet, a child being raised for the order; a practice that the Jesuits <note>A comparison to the Society of Jesus, a Catholic religious order founded in the 16th century, known for their educational systems involving young students.</note> have since followed.

Throughout, the statutes show a spirit of thrift regarding clothing; but this is another point on which the facts do not agree with the law. Nothing is more certain than the luxury of the Templars.

## II. *Of the Chaplains.*

At first, there were only knights in the Order, and they were subject, for everything concerning religion, to the Patriarch of Jerusalem <note>The highest-ranking bishop in the Latin Church of the Holy Land.</note>

Jerusalem, and, with his agreement, to the bishops of the dioceses where they held their property and their houses. The Knights of the Hospital (later of Malta) having obtained several privileges from the Pope—and notably the exemption for the Order and its priests from episcopal jurisdiction <term>episcopal jurisdiction: the legal authority and oversight that a local bishop exercises over the clergy and religious institutions within his territory</term>—the Templars aspired to the same independence and obtained it successively. Forty or fifty years after the foundation of the Order, the Pope took it under his immediate protection and ordered that it should admit priests and religious members into its ranks.

The reception of priests was the same as that of the knights, with the exception of certain questions regarding nobility and knighthood, which were not required of them. They took the same vows, or at least there is every reason to presume so. There was some difference in their dress, and a sort of distinctive mark, called a *barette* <note>original: "barette"; a type of cap or headpiece worn by clergy, from which the modern biretta evolved</note> in the trial records.

There were also Templar bishops.

The knights wore long beards, following the custom of the time; but it was prescribed for the clerics <term>clerics: members of the clergy, specifically those in the Order who were ordained priests rather than fighting knights</term> to be clean-shaven.

The priests wore gloves; this was a practice devised out of respect for consecration <note>original: "consécration"; the ritual act of making something holy. In this context, it refers to the belief that a priest's hands, having been consecrated to handle the Eucharist, should be covered or protected</note>.

The chaplains of the Temple were not great in number; and within the houses of the Order, many secular priests <term>secular priests: clergy who live "in the world" under a bishop, rather than belonging to a specific religious order like the Templars</term> still lived: these men themselves held important ecclesiastical privileges.

Within the houses of the Order, the priests held honorary prerogatives, such as a seat in the chapter <term>chapter: the formal assembly of the members of a religious house or order for business and discipline</term>, being served first in the refectory <term>refectory: the communal dining hall</term>, etc.; they could attain high offices and enter into the government of the Order.

They were subject to the same discipline, but treated less severely than the other brothers.

### III. *Of the Serving Brothers.*

At the time of the Order’s foundation, and even for some time after its regular formation, there were no servants; but as the number of its knights increased, and hired squires and valets no longer sufficed, practical and political reasons led to the creation of a class of brothers destined for various services, both external and internal, for the Order and its knights.

### IV. *Of Persons attached to the Order.*

In those times when it was within a prelate's power to place an interdict <term>interdict: a religious censure that prohibited a person or an entire region from participating in most church services and sacraments</term> upon an entire city or a whole district, people were eager to exempt themselves from these rigors through affiliation with a privileged and powerful Order.

Historians of the Templars have paid too little attention to these connections between the Temple and outsiders: one saw within it people of the world of both sexes, as well as clerics living in the world <note>secular clergy who lived in society rather than in a monastery</note>.

The affiliates of the Temple resembled the tertiaries <term>tertiaries: lay members of a religious order who do not take full monastic vows but follow the order's spirit in their daily lives</term> of the mendicant orders <term>mendicant orders: Christian religious orders, like the Franciscans and Dominicans, whose members adopted a lifestyle of poverty and traveled to preach</term>. Among the Dominicans, these tertiaries served effectively to maintain the Inquisition. The same is true of the temporal Jesuits <note>lay associates who supported the Society of Jesus</note>, whose existence has been proven.

The Rule of the Temple speaks of married brothers; the testimony of Raynald Bergeron proves that they existed. Innocent III, in a bull <term>bull: a formal public decree or charter issued by the Pope</term>, boasts of being an affiliate of the Temple. Philip the Fair <note>Philip IV of France, the king who eventually orchestrated the Order's destruction</note> wrote to the Pope that he and his nephew had sought to become confreres <note>lay associates or "brothers" who shared in the spiritual merits of the Order</note> of the Temple.

### VI. *On the Dignities of the Order.*

The Grand Master held the rank of prince among kings. In councils, he took his place after the bishops and before the ambassadors.

The other dignitaries were the Grand Prior, the <term>seneschal: the second-in-command to the Grand Master, responsible for administrative duties and acting as his deputy</term>, the marshal, the treasurer, the <term>draper: the officer responsible for the distribution of clothing and linens to the members of the Order</term>, the <term>turcopolier</term> (this was the general of the light cavalry, which in the East was called a <term>turcopole: light cavalry troops often recruited locally in the Levant and equipped in the Turkish fashion</term>), and the <term>bailiff: a high-ranking official who oversaw specific territories or administrative districts</term> of Jerusalem.

There were, in addition, Visitors-General, a high office whose power was temporary. The visitor of a province extended his jurisdiction over the neighboring province.

Every superior had a knight as a brother-in-arms. (This was a blend of religious chivalry with military chivalry, which was not insignificant in ensuring the safety of these leaders.)

The provincial masters, whose provisional power was very great, took a special oath in this capacity. Every provincial master had two knights as assistants. Below him were the bailiffs and priors...

### VII. Internal Administration.

The Grand Master holds the place of God. This expression, common to many rules of religious orders <note>Refers to the strict vows of obedience taken by monks and knights, where the superior represents divine authority</note>, did not prevent the administration from being a blend of aristocracy—at least according to the law and in form—as the Grand Master was considered subject to the <term>General Chapters: the high-level legislative assemblies of the Order where major policy and personnel decisions were made</term>, just as the Pope is to the councils of the Church. The Grand Master held the title of <term>Vicar-General: a representative acting with the full authority of the Pope in specific matters</term> of the Pope.

Decisions made in the council (<note>original: "konvent"</note>) in Jerusalem by all those who held a seat there, or in a general chapter, became law for the entire Order.

The general chapters were very secret, but they were held rarely; for they were very expensive to convene, and the Grand Master feared them no less than the Pope feared the church councils.

The Council of the Temple, which governed in the intervals between general chapters, was composed of the Grand Master, the high dignitaries, and the provincial masters—

What the Grand Master’s council was to the entire Order, the provincial master’s council was to the province, located in the seat of the <term>Bailiwick: the administrative district or jurisdiction governed by a bailiff</term> where the master resided.

Every house of the <term>Priory: a religious house or monastery under the authority of a prior</term> or large <term>Commandery: a landed estate or manor under the control of a Knight Templar</term> had its own chapter, presided over by the bailiff of the prior. Careful watch was kept to ensure these subordinate leaders did not exceed their power.

### VIII. *Relations of the Order of the Temple with other Orders.*

Although, in the statutes, every word breathes a spirit of good harmony between the Order of the Temple and that of the Hospital, they were nonetheless very divided in later times. As early as the end of the 12th century, one sees the <term>Hospitallers: The Order of Knights of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem, the Templars' primary rivals</term> attacking the Templars to support one of their vassals who had been dispossessed by the latter. The histories of <term>Malta: A reference to the Hospitallers, who later became known as the Knights of Malta</term> are filled with the battles they fought against one another. The historian of the Temple (who is merely an often very clumsy <term>apologist: someone who writes in defense of a particular cause or institution</term>) denies these discords in vain. Examples of defectors moving from one Order to the other are common (even though the statutes seem to oppose such moves.)

As for the <term>Teutonic Order: A German medieval military order modeled after the Templars</term>, it is singular that it is never mentioned in the statutes; especially since this Order had emerged from the Temple itself, and its confirmation by the Pope was requested by the Grand Master <note>Gerard de Ridefort (c. 1140–1189), a Grand Master known for his influence and his role in the disastrous Battle of Hattin.</note> Riderfort. This is explained by the need the Dominicans had for the Templars in order to gain standing among illustrious families. ### IX. Concerning the Privileges of the Temple.

Privileges were the foundations of the popes' dominance. Religious societies that the pope exempted from <term>episcopal jurisdictions: The legal authority and oversight of local bishops</term> were, for that reason, more devoted to him.

More than thirty years passed before the Templars obtained the slightest favor from the popes. (This is further proof of the purely military purpose of the Order) (1). If they were very late in being removed from the authority of the bishops, it can be attributed to the influence of <term>Saint Bernard: Bernard of Clairvaux, the influential Cistercian abbot who drafted the Latin Rule of the Templars and generally opposed the exemption of monks from their bishops’ control</term>, who disapproved of this type of privilege.

The <term>papal bull: An official decree or charter issued by the Pope</term> of Alexander III, from 1172, secured this exemption for them. It is the same decree that forbade the brothers from leaving the Order without the consent of the grand master.

The Templars were permitted to have Mass celebrated in all places placed under <term>interdict: A church penalty that suspended religious services in a specific district or country, usually as a result of a conflict between the Pope and a local ruler</term>.

A priest of the Temple had the power to grant absolution <note>original: "absoudre"</note> with the same authority as a bishop.

# APOLOGETIC DISSERTATION
## *On the primary accusations that were raised against the Order of the Templars.*

### I. INTRODUCTION.

The primary grievances with which the enemies of this Order claimed to justify its destruction were such that, once they were proven, there remained no means of saving even its honor, neither in those times nor in those to come. Everything that could most incite moral and religious indignation was gathered there: the renunciation of God and of Christ, spitting upon the cross, the contempt for and violation of two sacraments <note>These likely refer to the sacraments of the Eucharist and Penance, which the Templars were accused of desecrating or mishandling.</note>, the worship of the Devil under the form of an idol, and finally, the unnatural vice <note>A common historical euphemism for sodomy, which was one of the central charges used by the French crown to discredit the Order.</note>, authorized by the very laws of the Order. Thus, although the plan so artfully devised and directed by King Philip the Fair <note>original: "Philippe-le-Bel"</note> and by his confessor, the Inquisitor William of Paris, failed in this regard—that even contemporaries were not

## II. The means by which the confessions *of the Templars* were obtained.

Since the confessions of the Templars themselves must provide the foundation for our research, it is appropriate to examine to what extent these confessions were freely given; all the more so because even those who felt they must use them against the accused could not deny that, at least in part, they had been forced. This is evident above all from the depositions <term>depositions: formal statements given under oath during a legal proceeding</term> of the French knights.

Let us first take a brief look at the treatment experienced by the Templars in the various countries where they were put on trial.

In a single day, by order of the King <note>Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair, who orchestrated the arrests on Friday, October 13, 1307.</note>, all were seized and thrown into prison. All the leaders of the Order, even the Grand Master <note>Jacques de Molay.</note>, were in France at that time. The plan had been kept so secret that very few brothers were able to escape their fate through prompt flight. Such a violent and illegal procedure against an Order that was answerable only to the Church, must

From the very preliminaries of these interrogations, one could see the partiality that would preside over them. Before anything was proven, the accused suffered the fate of convicted criminals. They found themselves incarcerated and put in irons. They were refused the necessities of life. Accustomed to the well-being and even the superfluity that their riches could provide, they were forced to subsist on a pension of 12 deniers <note>The denier was a medieval penny; 12 deniers equaled one sou, representing a meager subsistence wage</note>, if indeed this provision—scarcely settled for their maintenance in 1309—was paid to them at all. One can easily see how, under such circumstances, the Templars themselves encouraged one another not to make themselves and their Order even more miserable through stubborn resistance. One can imagine how they came to coordinate their confessions among themselves, or to subscribe to those prescribed by their jailers—especially when, around the same time, by order of the Council of Sens <note>The Council of Sens in 1310 was a provincial church council that notoriously sentenced fifty-four Templars to be burned at the stake as "relapsed heretics" because they had retracted confessions previously extracted under torture.</note>, fifty-four brothers were burned in Paris. At that time, threats were also made in the name of the Pope of a similar fate for all those who would not confess; while those who obeyed the King would be set free. Is it then surprising that most of the Templars interrogated in Paris confessed to the main charges, and that many depositions are expressed in almost the same terms?

This consistency naturally struck the Papal Commission. It gave rise to the undoubtedly well-intentioned question put to the prisoners: namely, whether they had been in any way—

### III. *Treatment experienced by the Templars, and results of the proceedings against them in other countries.*

One can easily perceive how, under such circumstances, the Templars themselves urged one another not to bring even greater misery upon themselves and their Order through stubborn resistance. We can understand how they came to coordinate their confessions among themselves, or to subscribe to those prescribed by their jailers—especially when, around the same time and by order of the Council of Sens <note>A provincial council held in Paris in 1310, led by the Archbishop of Sens, who was a close ally of the King.</note>, fifty-four brothers were burned at the stake in Paris. Is it any wonder, then, that most of the Templars interrogated in Paris confessed to the primary charges, and that many of the depositions were phrased in nearly identical terms?

## IV. SICILY.

The king protected the Order. We do not possess the interrogations of the knights themselves, but only those of a few witnesses. The result of these records is that the voice of the people declared itself in favor of the Templars.

## V. GERMANY.

Their innocence was recognized by the Council of Mainz <note>A powerful archbishopric and center of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> and by the provincial council of Trier. # Historical Memoirs

At the time of the trial of the Templars, the emperor and the Empire were making preparations against him <note>Referring to Philip IV ("the Fair") of France, whose territorial and political ambitions threatened the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. The knights were only mistreated in Magdeburg, whose archbishop—a friend and table-companion of the Gascon Pope Clement V <note>Clement V was the first pope of the "Avignon Papacy," often seen as a puppet of the French king.</note>—was subject to French influence. In Trier, whose archbishop <note>Baldwin of Luxembourg, a powerful prince-elector.</note>, the brother of Emperor Henry VII, held an entirely opposite opinion, there was not a single deposition <term>deposition: a formal statement of testimony used as evidence in a legal proceeding.</term> contrary to the Order.

Such was the outcome of the prosecutions against the Templars in various countries; from this arises, at the very least, a well-founded doubt that their condemnation in France was legitimate. We have already seen that the French depositions were far from being free of foreign influence, and that they were largely forced <note>A reference to the widespread use of torture by the French Inquisition to extract confessions.</note>: but I do not wish to prejudice the reader.

The examination of the main heads of accusation will be, I hope, no less favorable to the Templars than the history of the trial. I shall pause here only at the main points. Regarding the imperial throne: The ambition of France, throughout the course of the 14th century, returned constantly to this plan <note>The French monarchy’s recurring attempt to claim the title of Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, which, in the 16th century, cost her so dearly <note>Likely referring to the costly and unsuccessful rivalry between Francis I of France and Charles V of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, and of which one still finds some traces in the policy of Louis XIV. I shall have the occasion to publish some curious research on this subject. (*Translator’s Note.*)

...of this Order had been public; but, contrary to the practice of other religious Orders, even the close relatives of the novice could not be present at the <term>taking of the habit: the formal ceremony where a candidate receives the official robes of the Order, marking their entry into communal life.</term> From this arose suspicions and plausible excuses for all sorts of accusations. For a long time, this secrecy had given rise to rumors unfavorable to the Order. When the grounds for complaint against them were being compiled, this one presented itself first. When questioned on this point, the Templars did not even think to defend it; yet, they could have easily justified this mystery, which, in fact, can be explained in two ways.

Secrecy and silence had characterized this entire institution from its very beginning. One can see, through all its laws, that everything occurring in a <term>chapter: a formal meeting or assembly of the members of the Order to discuss business or discipline.</term> was considered a <term>chapter secret: internal matters that members were strictly forbidden from disclosing to the public.</term> (1). Furthermore, the secrecy of the reception was a symbol that signaled to the new brother his separation from the secular world and his new obligations.

But, by a natural connection, since this mystery aligns in some way with the other grievances against the Order, it is these grievances themselves that must be addressed in order to dismantle them.

4. How did such grave crimes, so contrary to the religious prejudices of those times, and even to the healthiest ideas of religion, arise against a completely innocent Body? The numerous victims who—especially among the noble class (1)—were still falling at the time of the Templars' trial, were like the seed that caused their sects to multiply. Thus, nothing was more natural, once one wished to prosecute the Templars as heretics, than to attribute to them these same errors—the only ones well known to their enemies. From these first records, sent to the inquisitor Guillaume <note>original: "Guillaume"; likely Guillaume de Paris, the Dominican Inquisitor of France and confessor to King Philip the Fair</note>, were drawn the famous one hundred and thirty-two articles—the basis for the final proceedings—in which one can see how flawed their sources were. Even if this attempt were nothing more than a hypothesis, I maintain that it is more plausible than any other, and that through the facts confirming it, it reaches historical truth as closely as possible.

The crucifixes displayed everywhere incited this multitude at every moment. But the more the inquisitors saw such opinions recur, the more they must have become entrenched in the idea that contempt for the cross was the common principle of all heretics. 2. Once it was established that the Templars worshipped the **Devil**, there was no longer any doubt that they were doing the work of the Demon: **sorcery**. He had studied in **Spain** among the <term>Moors</term> <note>The Muslim inhabitants of the Iberian Peninsula; medieval scholars often traveled to Moorish Spain to study advanced science and philosophy</note>; from them he acquired his talents for **mechanics** (1).

If such was the judgment of the greatest men of those times on **witchcraft** and **magic** (for they were hardly separated), it is not surprising that the multitude was no more enlightened, and that their very brilliance caused these same men to be counted among famous magicians.

These were abundant in those times. They were forged or cast according to specific magical proportions, at certain hours of the day, under specific constellations, and even while summoning evil spirits (2); afterward, they were consecrated for use in magic. This consecration was called *baptism*; not because it was based on the Catholic practice of baptizing certain objects used in divine service, but under the assumption that the Devil was the ape of God <note>The "Ape of God" is a medieval concept describing how the Devil mocks God by imitating holy rituals in a distorted way</note>. Even the name *Abraxas* decides nothing, since it is found on stones that are evidently pagan, and it could have been used just as well in the mysteries of the pagan Gnostics as in those of the Christian Gnostics.

As for the assertion "that the name *Baffometus* <note>original: Baffometus; a Latinized form of Baphomet</note> does not belong to the image, but to a hieroglyph imprinted upon it," it rests on only a single testimony, so brief and so un-

...complete <note>referring to the etymological explanation of "Baphomet" started on the previous page</note>, and that it holds no more weight than other completely different interpretations (1).

The Greek origin of the name *Baphe metous* <note>original Greek: βαφη μητους; Nicolaï interpreted this as "baptism of wisdom" or "tincture of the mind"</note> can hardly be judged by the standards of secular writers. If all other evidence aligned, this point might be overlooked. However, from where could the Templars have received such a name? In the East at that time, the dominant languages were Arabic and Syriac. The Greeks were never friends of the Order. Furthermore, the Manichaean <term>followers of a dualistic belief system that saw the world as a struggle between light and dark</term> sects of the West had, as far as is known, preserved no Greek terms from the ancient Gnostics or Manichaeans. Add to this that the master, when presenting the idol, is said to have pronounced the Arabic words *Y Alla* <note>original: *Y Alla*, likely a transcription of "Ya Allah," meaning "O God"</note>. What are we to make of this mixture? There is no doubt that the Templars understood Arabic better than Greek. Yet, to base such a significant claim on a single deposition <term>a formal statement used as evidence in a legal trial</term> is to risk too much.

Nonetheless, even if we admit that everything could be explained through external considerations, the primary question remains: did the Templars possess a secret Gnostic doctrine?

This can only be answered through historical research; and first, the constitution <term>the foundational rules and laws governing the Order</term> of the Order must be rigorously weighed. But this constitution, which now, by—

every appearance that the Templars, or at least the French ones, effectively neglected the <term>elevation</term> <note>The ritual of lifting the consecrated bread and wine for the congregation to see and adore.</note>; this provided a fine pretext for their enemies to assume the total omission of the consecration. Now, it seems very probable here that the Templars may have borrowed a practice from **Cîteaux**. For a long time, this Order, following the ancient rite of the Church, abstained from presenting the host and the chalice for the adoration of the people after the consecration. It was in 1215 that for the first time, as a result of the **Lateran Council**, the elevation was recommended (1). This ancient observance had undoubtedly received the approval of **St. Bernard**, a defender of <term>positive theology</term> <note>A branch of theology that relies on established authorities—Scripture, Church Fathers, and Councils—rather than speculative reasoning.</note>, and who, without denying the presence of Christ in the **Eucharist**, admitted it only in a mystical sense (2). *absolution from sins* <note>original: "absolutio à peccatis"</note>, which is <term>sacramental</term> <note>Relating to a religious rite, like confession, which is believed to convey divine grace and requires an ordained priest.</note> and requires personal <term>consecration</term> <note>The formal act of making someone a priest, setting them apart for sacred duties.</note>, but only *absolution from the infractions of the rule* <note>original: "absolutio ab excessibus regularium"</note>, for which these leaders were fully authorized. The same is true for the forms of absolution reported in the <term>trial</term> <note>Refers to the infamous trial of the Templars (1307–1312) initiated by King Philip IV of France.</note>; one always finds there these reservations: — *By the authority handed down to him.* <note>original: "Auctoritate sibi traditâ."</note> — *By the power granted to him by God and the Lord Pope, insofar as he is able.* <note>original: "Ex potestate sibi concessâ à Deo et Domino papâ in quantum potest."</note> — *I forgive insofar as it lies within me.* <note>original: "Remitto quantum in me est."</note> — Even the French witnesses only speak of the forgiveness that the leaders can and must give for disciplinary matters.

If the power to absolve seems to increase according to the rank of the leader, the formula used alone proves that they were far from wanting to exceed their rightful authority.

(1) In a very curious note, Mr. Münter suggests a second motive for this rupture.

It concerns an Order of chivalry founded by the Dominicans themselves under various names, including that of **Knights of Saint Dominic**, and more notoriously still under the Italian title of **Cavalieri Gaudenti** <note>Italian: "Joyous Knights." Originally the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary, they were nicknamed "Gaudenti" because they were perceived as enjoying a comfortable, secular life compared to stricter monks.</note>. A learned Dominican named **Federici** published a major history of these **Joyous Knights** in 1787. This order was founded in 1209, during the crusade of Simon de Montfort against the **Albigensians** <note>A group of religious dissidents in southern France who were the target of a brutal crusade and the first medieval Inquisition.</note>, and was placed under the direction of the Dominicans by Pope Innocent III, who had confirmed and favored it. The Dominicans had spread this order into Italy. Faithful to the example of its founders, this Order worked with them toward the destruction of heretics—if not with the sword, then at least by every other possible means. Consequently, the **Joyous Knights** took part in the trial of the Templars, and, as was only fair, they were given a share of the remains of the Order. Their historian, who states explicitly that some of the Templars’ property fell to them, gives as a reason that several Templars entered this society after the suppression of their own. From the fact that their admission was tolerated by the Dominicans, one might draw some inference regarding the innocence of the condemned. The end of the 13th<gloss>th</gloss> century, when the **Joyous Knights** multiplied greatly, must be the era of the falling out between the Templars and the Dominicans.

# PREFACE.

**I**n a subject that was hardly favorable, and above all very difficult to treat, the author of the tragedy of the Templars <note>This refers to the 1805 play *Les Templiers* by François-Just-Marie Raynouard, which was a massive theatrical success in Napoleonic France.</note> has achieved the most brilliant success. He has stirred souls and elevated minds. Reading his play will crown the honors of its performance. His style—energetic without being harsh or bloated, eloquent without declamation, and precise without being obscure—can only ensure that the printed version is received as favorably as the performance; a certain wit at the court of Louis XIV once called printing *a civil petition against public approval* <note>original: "une requête civile contre l'approbation publique." This phrase, attributed to the Marquis de Lassay, implies that while a play might succeed through the raw emotion of a live performance, the printed text serves as a formal appeal to the reader's sober judgment.</note>. M. <term>Raynouard</term> <note>François-Just-Marie Raynouard (1761–1836) was a French dramatist and historian who famously defended the innocence of the Templars.</note> has thus won his case twice: but he wishes to win it a third time by maintaining the innocence of the <term>Templars</term> <note>The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, a wealthy and powerful military order suppressed by Pope Clement V and King Philip IV of France in the early 14th century.</note> as an evident fact and a palpable truth. It seems that this evidence is not at all necessary to his merit, and that his beautiful verses could well do without his skillful legal defense.

### Historical Memoirs

Who, indeed, ever demanded that historical tragedy be literally modeled on history? When Voltaire was reproached for making **Mahomet** <note>This refers to Voltaire’s 1741 play *Le fanatisme, ou Mahomet le Prophète*. It is, with even greater reason, the privilege of the dramatic poet to ennoble the character he brings to the stage. It is heroism that he comes to offer as an example to mankind. What does the name of the hero matter? It was enough for Mr. R*** <note>François-Just-Marie Raynouard (1761–1836), the author of the play in question.</note> that his characters were not evidently guilty, and had been manifestly oppressed. He knew how to make them admired; they were sufficiently absolved.

Two pitfalls are difficult for <term>scholars: Here referring to "érudits," the specialized historians and researchers of the 18th and 19th centuries who focused on primary sources and antiquities.</term> to avoid: the abuse of detail and the abuse of research. The first only makes them tedious; by the second, they become fanciful and sometimes ridiculous. History has not yet accurately portrayed this monarch, who has to his credit many actions similar to those of Louis XI <note>King of France from 1461 to 1483, known for his cunning and consolidating royal power</note>, and who caused as much harm to France as the latter has since repaired. ## *The spirit and specific intent of the first act of authority against the Knights Templar.*

Innocent III <note>Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216), who significantly expanded the secular power of the papacy</note>, the most skillful, in my view, of all the Roman pontiffs, had first conceived the idea of turning Christians against Christians in a crusade <note>A reference to the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) directed against the Cathar heretics in Southern France</note>, a murderous invention that defined the thirteenth century. The Popes did not have the honor of this discovery: Philip IV <note>Philip the Fair (r. 1285–1314)</note> beat them to it. ### CHAPTER V.

->*The Pope's Goodwill Harmed the Accused.*<-

Unfortunately, the Pope was not the only one deceived by the Court <note>The Royal Court of King Philip IV "the Fair" of France</note>: it is highly likely that the respect that was feigned for his authority also misled the Templars. This is what I can discern in several circumstances of the second <term>proceeding</term> <note>The formal legal inquiry, specifically the papal commission intended to investigate the Order as a whole</note>.

Nothing was more natural than for these unfortunate men to look to the Pope as their support. The vigor of his initial protests, the complaints he made in his <term>bulls</term> <note>Official edicts or decrees issued by the Pope</note> about the violent means used to extort their confessions, the precautions he seemed to have taken for their safety, the establishment of this papal commission to examine the case of the Order in general, and the appeal made to all those among the brothers who wished to defend their body <note>Refers to the collective organization of the Order</note>—all of this combined to convince them of the reluctance with which he would sacrifice them; and they must have hoped for much from the efforts he would make to save them. They at least expected more equitable methods in this final proceeding.

### On the Templars

The precaution taken by the papal commissioners, from the very start of their proceedings, is quite remarkable: they added to the oath of the deponents <note>Individuals giving testimony or statements under oath</note> that they must keep their depositions <note>Official statements or testimonies</note> secret. We see elsewhere that the intent was to prevent them from coordinating their testimonies; from this, it follows that the prisoners hoped to strengthen their defense through such cooperation and to impress both their enemies and their judges.

On the other hand, it further appears that those Templars who so loudly retracted their initial confessions before the council were emboldened by these hopes and driven by this agreement among themselves. These numerous retractions were, in fact, necessary to serve as the foundation for the defense strategy they intended to follow: for how could the Templars appearing before the commission <note>The papal commission investigating the Order as an institution</note> have maintained the innocence of the Order and the claim that confessions were extorted <note>Obtained through force or torture</note>, if at the same time the Templars brought before the council <note>Provincial councils, such as the Council of Sens in Paris, which judged individual members</note> had all confirmed those very same statements? Neither group supposed at the time that the two tribunals were acting under different influences; and it is clear that the Pope’s reputed goodwill was a mere illusion to them.

## CHAPTER VI.

### Fatal Effects of This Confidence.

A striking result of the judgments passed by the provincial councils <note>Regional gatherings of church leaders to settle disciplinary or doctrinal matters.</note>—particularly the Council of Sens, which met in Paris—reveals the nature of this disastrous misunderstanding. Among the five classes of persons distinguished there, against whom measures were taken with varying severity, only one was declared worthy of death and handed over to the secular arm <term>secular arm: the civil authorities responsible for carrying out physical punishments or executions, as the Church was officially prohibited from shedding blood</term>. Anyone viewing these events through the light of simple common sense would initially believe that punishment should be reserved for those who confess to crimes rather than those who deny them. Yet the opposite was decreed; an absurd barbarity that was made logically consistent by a single word: ***relapsed***. 

Who were these "relapsed" individuals? They were those who retracted their confessions, whether those confessions had been extorted <note>Obtained through torture or threats.</note> or given voluntarily. However, this term, based on its Latin etymology <note>original: "relapsus," meaning "one who has fallen back."</note>, denotes only one who falls back into heresy <note>Beliefs or opinions contrary to orthodox religious doctrine.</note> after having formally abjured <note>To solemnly renounce or recant a belief.</note> it. It seemed difficult for someone who simply retracted a statement to be considered "relapsed": how could they be judged as such? It was through a legal extension, a fiction so hateful that at the time, neither the accused nor anyone else could have anticipated it.

<summary>This page explains the "relapsed" legal trap where Templars who retracted their confessions were sentenced to death, showing how their attempt at a legal defense backfired.</summary>

# On the Templars.

Although for a hundred years, the jurisprudence of the Inquisition had had time to perfect itself, it seems that this final refinement was still lacking; it is owed to Philip <note>King Philip IV "the Fair" of France (reigned 1285–1314), who orchestrated the downfall of the Templars.</note> and the French clergy. We see from the acts of the trial that the council addressed the Pope himself to submit this question: **whether such a revocation can be called a relapse?** <note>original: "utrum talis revocatio possit dici relapsio?"</note>. He replied with these evasive expressions: "You know the written laws; proceed according to the law." This was a way of washing his hands of the matter, like the Roman Pontius Pilate. The bishops, animated by a very Pharisaical spirit <note>A reference to the Pharisees of the New Testament, implying a rigid, hypocritical adherence to the letter of the law while ignoring its spirit of justice.</note>, had little regard for the circumspection of the head of the Church; they decided in the affirmative. 

But after this decision, it still remained to be seen whether it could be given a retroactive effect by applying it to the Templars. The judges did not doubt it for a moment, if indeed any scruple even occurred to them; <term>canon law: the internal ecclesiastical law governing the Catholic Church</term> lent itself to everything. Finally, this word ***relapsed*** lit more than a hundred pyres in the city of Paris alone; this word (1) was like being ***outlawed*** during our own days of revolutionary terror—those sinister days <note>A reference to the "Reign of Terror" during the French Revolution (1793–1794) where the label "hors la loi" (outlaw) meant immediate execution without trial.</note>.

***

(1) After the revocation of the Edict of Nantes <note>The 1685 decree by Louis XIV that stripped French Protestants (Huguenots) of their rights, leading to persecution.</note>, this same word had effects no less murderous and no less barbaric. See Rhulières, *Historical Clarifications on the Causes of the Revocation*, etc. 1788.

The Pope was therefore nothing more than a figurehead for the King—or rather, the King acted as Pope himself. This equivocal state of affairs, the ambiguity of the proceedings, and the uncertainty of the outcomes were so many traps for the Templars, dragging a great number of them to their deaths; for if none of them had retracted <note>This refers to the Templars withdrawing their initial confessions, which had often been obtained through torture. But who can tell us what these "variations" <note>original: "variations"; in this context, it refers to inconsistencies or changes in a witness's testimony</note> were, and before which authority they had taken place? Was it before the cardinals at Chinon? No; for that would have been to contradict the report they had made to the Pope, which could not have been done in such an assembly. But, as the very purpose of the assembly indicates, the task then was to prepare for the new legal proceedings. They intended to make use of the Grand Master's <note>Jacques de Molay, the last Grand Master of the Knights Templar</note> testimony there. But, whether he had regained his courage, like the others and for the same reasons, or whether, out of a whim of corporate pride and chivalric honor, he was loath to publicly support confessions harmful to his society, one must believe that in the preliminary talks, he had shown himself determined to hold, should he be forced to, a different language.

This is what was called "varying." These were certain reservations or modifications that he intended to have admitted, and which were rejected by deciding that they would stick to the initial answers that were consistent with those of all his brothers. This word "variation" was, moreover, important in comparison with "retraction." For the latter would have made him a <term>relapsed heretic</term> <note>original: "relaps"; in the Inquisition, a person who recanted their confession was considered to have "fallen back" into heresy, a crime punishable by death</note> and would have led him to the stake: something which, at that time, they wished to avoid.

Until that terrible moment, the Grand Master’s <note>Jacques de Molay, the last Grand Master of the Knights Templar</note> variations indeed continued. Before he appeared exposed on a scaffold in the middle of the square of Notre-Dame, and before that retraction which was so truly unexpected—according to the account of the continuer of Nangis <note>The "continuer of Nangis" refers to the anonymous monks who continued the historical chronicles of Guillaume de Nangis after his death in 1300</note>—only a few days earlier, in a large assembly, he had once again persisted in his first confession. ## CHAPTER VIII.

### Conduct of the Trial.

I can easily understand how, despite all the defenses <note>original: "apologies"; here used in the classical sense of a formal justification or legal defense</note> written on their behalf, many people remain sincerely convinced that the accusations against the Templars had some foundation. However, if one studies the trial even slightly, they will become even more convinced that it was conducted with profound cunning and atrocious immorality. All sincere historians have sensed this. Yet, there is no shortage of courtier writers <note>authors who wrote specifically to flatter the ruling monarch or political powers</note> who have denied or concealed it. As if every modern power shared a common cause with the powers of the past, and as if praising the former were a sure way to please the latter, the persecutors of the Templars still find eager defenders today. It is therefore necessary, in turn, to formally accuse these persecutors and to reveal their conspiracy through tangible evidence. If I can untangle the hateful craft that directed the proceedings within the details of the trial, and if I provide clear evidence instead of the vague assumptions previously held, I will not have wasted my time or that of the reader.

Let us suppose that the prince <note>King Philip IV, also known as Philip the Fair</note>, the ministers, the nobles, the prelates, the doctors, and the monks conspired for the destruction of the Templars and

The plan for the trial was laid out in such a way as to achieve two essential objectives.

1st. The court wanted to remain in control of the case: to do so, it was necessary that the matter did not leave the jurisdiction of what was called the *ordinary* <term>ordinary: the standard legal authority held by a local bishop over his diocese</term>, meaning the diocesan bishops along with the inquisitor; furthermore, it had to permit the prosecution, or at least the assistance, of the secular authority <note>This refers to the royal officials of King Philip IV "the Fair" of France, who orchestrated the arrests.</note>. It was necessary to remove the trial from the direct oversight of the Holy See <term>Holy See: the central administration of the Catholic Church and the office of the Pope</term>: it was even necessary to intimidate the Pope enough so that he could not offer the accused any open protection. The accusation and the crime of heresy achieved all these effects; thus, provided that heresy was proven (1), any other error or disorder was, in a way, merely auxiliary, serving only to strengthen the cry of public condemnation and anathema <term>anathema: a formal curse or excommunication by the Church, often carrying social and legal weight</term>.

### *Preliminaries of the Trial.*

# CHAPTER X.

## *Reflections on the preceding matters.*

I must address two reflections that naturally arise upon viewing this set of so well-coordinated measures.

1st. One might ask why there was so much craft, preparation, and care for an undertaking that seemed so easy in its execution; but bear in mind that Philip succeeded so easily only because his means were so well-combined. Such are those works which have cost all the more labor the more they display ease of execution. Furthermore, Philip had gathered so many extraordinary means only because he mistrusted the simple resources of authority; and he did so with great reason. His <term>exactions: Harsh demands or illegal taxes forced upon the people to fund royal ambitions.</term>, his <term>debased currency: Philip IV was nicknamed "the Counterfeiter" because he frequently reduced the silver content of French coins to manage his debts, leading to economic instability.</term>, his breaches of faith, his encroachments on the rights of all classes, his violence, and his pride had made him detested. Local revolts had broken out. Certain that all his operations could only encounter unfavorable prejudices, he had to neglect nothing to surround this one <note>The "one" refers to the arrest and trial of the Knights Templar.</note> with all the supports of force and prestige.

2nd. One will be astonished to find a malice so

refined, maneuvers so subtle in an age so ignorant and so crude; but what can we conclude from this? Only that which all history demonstrates: that the art of harming humans, of corrupting them, or of deceiving them, has nothing in common with the sciences that serve, enlighten, and improve them. Or rather, that this art is quite easy and quite despicable, since the most barbarous excel at it just as much as the most civilized. ## C H A P T E R  X I.

### What were the King’s motives.

We now see with sufficient clarity how <term>Philip the Fair: Philip IV (1268–1314), the King of France who famously engineered the downfall of the Templars to consolidate his power and wealth.</term> destroyed the <term>Templars: A wealthy and powerful Catholic military order established during the Crusades, which became a target of the French crown in the early 14th century.</term> as soon as he resolved to destroy them. But why did he wish to do so? What interests, what passions gave this resolve such a terrible energy? Was vengeance his sole motive? Did fanaticism play no part in his animosity? Did a jealous policy dictate the decree? Or was greed the primary instigator? Shall we rank the judicial massacre of the Templars among those coups d’état that <term>Aristotle: The ancient Greek philosopher whose political theories were frequently cited by medieval and early modern scholars to analyze the behavior of rulers.</term> so rightly calls the *sophisms of princes*, since one can only mask their indignity through false applications of the grand phrase ***public safety*** <note>original: "salut public"</note>, or through even falser distinctions between the morality of governments and private morality? Or should we see in it only a plunder very similar to the ***extortions*** <note>original: "avanies," a term often used historically to describe the arbitrary taxes or fines imposed by Ottoman authorities on European merchants.</note> practiced by the **Turkish Pashas**, the **Mamluks**, or the **Moors of Morocco**—and entirely similar to the proscription of the **Jews** which preceded it, as well as that of the **Lepers** which followed? <note>King Philip IV expelled the Jews from France in 1306 to seize their property, and his reign (along with his sons') saw the "Lepers' Plot" of 1321, which led to the mass persecution of those with leprosy.</note> Must we say of the Templars what <term>Mézeray: François-Eudes de Mézeray (1610–1683), a French historian whose "History of France" was a standard reference during the author's time.</term> says...

## CHAPTER XII.

### *Testimonies and Judgments of Historians.*

I will not waste time discussing the alleged proofs that have been given for the selflessness of Philip the Fair <note>King Philip IV of France (r. 1285–1314), who was heavily in debt and sought to seize the Templars' vast wealth.</note>. What does it matter, for example, if after reaching an agreement with him, the Pope attests that his *dear son* <note>original: *cher fils*</note> did not act *out of greed* <note>original: *par avarice*</note>? It is as if the King were telling us so himself. From that moment on, Clement <note>Pope Clement V (r. 1305–1314), the first of the Avignon Popes, who was largely seen as a tool of the French monarchy.</note> did not write a single line that had not been pre-arranged. Furthermore, the few facts cited to absolve him of robbery are the very ones that convict him of it. It would remain to line up, so to speak, the authorities for and against, and to set them against one another. This method would be entirely to my advantage. Even among the historians who approved of the destruction of the Templars, many do not doubt the looting of their property; and those who justify the Order are so numerous that, among foreigners alone, more than forty are cited. But if the patience required for these long enumerations and meticulous comparisons is a merit, it must be admitted that it generally costs more than it re-

# C H A P T E R  X I I I.

## *Inquiry into the Wealth of the Order of the Temple.*

The assessment of this wealth is a necessary piece of data in the examination of this historical problem, and it is singular that no one has thought to obtain it. What follows will show, however, that the search is not at all fanciful, and that one can arrive at least at very close approximations of the actual figures.

As early as the year 1182, fifty years after its formal institution, there existed no potentates in Europe as wealthy as the Order of the Temple (1). Their assets did not cease to increase during the course of the thirteenth century.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### *The King's share of the spoils.*

Once the size and nature of the Order's spoils are understood, I believe we can see quite clearly what advantages were gained, especially in France, from their condemnation. The number of commanderies <note>original: "commanderies" — administrative centers or estates belonging to a military order, which functioned as the heart of their local economic and religious activity.</note> they possessed there has been estimated at two thousand. Although the exact definition of this title is not precisely known, it must indicate an estate of some significance. These land revenues were collected by the king's commissioners, and consequently for his profit, from the year 1307 until the assets were handed over to the Knights of the Hospital <note>original: "chevaliers de l'Hôpital" — a military-religious order, the Hospitallers, who eventually inherited much of the Templars' property. They later became known as the Knights of Rhodes and the Knights of Malta.</note> (later of Rhodes and of Malta). **Vertot** <note>René-Aubert Vertot (1655–1735), a French historian known for his works on the Knights of Malta</note> finds in this Memorandum proof that **Philip the Fair** profited from the assets of the Order. **Griffet** <note>Henri Griffet (1698–1771), a Jesuit historian</note> says that since all of this was nothing more than a simple project, it deserves no consideration. **Ramon Llull**, of Barcelona, had long engaged in trade in the **Levant** <note>The Eastern Mediterranean region</note>, as had **Sanudo**, who was Venetian.

What happened in Portugal deserves particular attention. One should not shy away from details when they provide a contrast that helps illuminate significant events.

King Denis <note>Dinis I of Portugal, reigned 1279–1325, known as the "Farmer King" or the "Troubadour King"</note>, a prince as firm as he was just and prudent, acted in every way as if he wished to contradict the contemporary princes of his time and evade the decrees of the Holy See <note>The jurisdiction and central administration of the Catholic Church, headed by the Pope</note>. The Templars had originally been called the *Knights of Christ*, a name always given to them by St. Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, a primary patron of the original Templar Order who wrote their Rule</note>: Denis therefore created an Order of Christ, which was endowed with their property. On their white habits, the Templars wore a long and wide red cross: this was preserved, by merely inserting a small white cross within its width. Far from proscribing the brothers of the Temple, they were required to join, and they were the first to be received into the new Order. The man who had been their national Grand Master, named Velasquez, was among the first provided with the commandery <note>An estate or manor under the control of a military order</note> of Montalvan. Even the word "abolition" was avoided. In a charter of 1317, it is stated that the Order of Christ is established *in reformation* <note>original Latin: "en reformation"; here implying a reorganization or renewal rather than a destruction</note> of that of the Temple. Not only did the first order receive the landed estates of the other; but the king also had delivered to the Grand Master of

## *On the Apologists of the Templars.*

The merit of a studious writer is useful and commendable when he gathers with choice and order, and stores up, so to speak, the facts and the monuments <note>original: "monumens"; in this period, the term refers to historical records, charters, and primary source documents rather than physical buildings</note> of history; if he also knows how to compare these pieces of information, to draw from them subtle and judicious conclusions, and to express their full instructive substance, this author is not yet worthy of the great name of historian; but his sagacity is a talent, a gift of art and nature; he has efforts to make; he requires a kind of courage: and as in any enterprise, the benefits must compensate for the risks, the pitfalls and difficulties of his own give him at least a right to the benevolent indulgence of the reader; a reflection which not only reassures me regarding everything I have said, but also emboldens me for what I have yet to say; for now is the moment to plunge into the occult <term>occultes: the hidden, secret, or esoteric aspects of the Order that were not revealed to the public</term> parts of the subject. ## C H A P T E R X V I I.

### *Can the Accusation Be Denied Entirely?*

While detractors have claimed to take advantage of the large number of confessions made by the knights themselves, others have responded by illustrating the harassment, torture, and deceptions used to extort these admissions. This response is solid and strong; yet, it must not be entirely sufficient, since at the same time, efforts are made to provide a favorable explanation for these same facts—which are claimed to have been confessed only under duress. Such acts include the denial of God or of Jesus Christ, and the desecration of the cross <note>These were the core charges of the trial: that recruits were forced to spit on the cross and deny Christ during their secret initiation.</note>. Pierre." If these depositions are nothing but absurd lies dictated to the <term>victims</term> <note>original: "patiens." In the context of historical legal proceedings, this refers specifically to those undergoing the "ordeal" or torture during interrogation.</note> by their executioners, why rack one’s brain to interpret them? Why not simply deny them outright? The reason is quite clear. It is because the sheer number of these depositions, and the uniformity of these confessions regarding the primary facts, give them a real weight—a consistency that shakes one's convictions despite oneself. Furthermore, many of these statements appear neither forced nor obtained through trickery; others are filled with such specific details that it is impossible for them to have all been invented and suggested to the witnesses. Certain circumstances cast a color of sincerity over what follows or precedes them that is entirely persuasive. Ultimately, if the collection of trial records leaves a general impression, it is certainly not one of the absolute falsehood of the accusations and confessions.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

->*New Research.*<-

An examination of everything that has been written about this great affair <note>The "great affair" refers to the sensational trial and eventual suppression of the Knights Templar by King Philip IV of France and Pope Clement V in the early 14th century.</note> shows that most of those who have discussed it were in more of a hurry to adopt a specific opinion, and to search through historical <term>records</term> <note>original: "monumens"; in this context, it refers to primary source documents, archives, and archaeological evidence rather than just physical statues.</note> for the means to defend their views or combat their adversaries, than to obtain a precise and complete knowledge of all those who were involved—both accusers and accused—and of everything in their lives that might have influenced the outcome. Or, if certain writers, such as Mr. Münter <note>Friedrich Münter (1761–1830), a Danish scholar and bishop who conducted extensive research into the secret statutes and history of the Templars.</note>, have truly delved into every part of the subject, they have still only treated it partially, and have not yet been able to illuminate it with all their insights. Since the understanding that books give us regarding the Order of the Temple and its knights is insufficient, how could we reach an agreement? I have already expanded upon this regarding one essential point. We shall now see that other facets of the subject are still shrouded in too much shadow.

But what is provided by neither the contemporaries nor the moderns <note>Referring to writers from the time of the Templars and historians from the author's own era.</note> is an exact idea of the singular power that such a society formed; for this idea is found in its underlying meaning, and not in the pages of books, which are more commonly copied than meditated upon. What purpose, then, has been served by those historians who have spent such prolix erudition <note>original: "prolixe érudition"; excessively wordy or dense scholarship.</note> verifying the dates of so many indifferent events? Most often, facts are gathered in histories like heaps of bones arranged in a vast cemetery. Many generations can be found there, but it is impossible to recognize a single man within them.

# CHAPTER XXI.

## *Number of the Templars. Power of the Order.*

A fourteenth-century Italian (1) says that fifteen thousand Templars were condemned. Even if this number were exaggerated, it can at least serve to estimate the total membership of the Order. A large portion had fled in France and especially in England. All the knights of Scotland had disappeared. Terms were reached <note>The author uses "on capitula," suggesting a negotiated surrender or settlement rather than a trial.</note> with those in Cyprus. They were acquitted in Flanders, Lorraine, Spain, and in half of Germany and Italy. Certainly, not even three-quarters of them were condemned. The ten to eleven thousand <term>commanderies: the administrative manors and estates managed by a commander of a military order</term> owned by the Order and their revenue provide an equally vast measure of its population. It is not a vague approximation to estimate the membership at more than twenty thousand, especially when including the brothers and the <term>servans: the "serving brothers" or non-knightly members who performed administrative or domestic duties</term>. This power grew by an immeasurable degree through the political and religious privileges with which this Order was invested. Well-endowed with land, the Templars exercised all the rights of nobles and lords within their territories. As knights, they enjoyed preeminences that made them the equals of princes. ## CHAPTER XXIII.

### *What could have been the ambition of the Order?*

I will admit it: this presumption would be better supported if I could demonstrate in the Order of the Temple an ambition equal to its power. In this regard, the facts prior to the trial provide nothing positive. However, they offer appearances significant enough that the suspicion was not considered completely baseless or senseless.

The overseas wars <note>The Crusades in the Holy Land.</note> had given birth to all these military monks <term>Military monks: Members of religious orders, like the Templars or Hospitallers, who took vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience but also served as elite soldiers.</term>. The preservation of Christian establishments in the East had allowed them to proliferate. It was for this sole purpose that princes and peoples never ceased to enrich them. Since the loss of the powerful city of Acre <note>The Fall of Acre in 1291 was a catastrophic event that marked the end of the Crusader states in the Levant, forcing the military orders to flee.</note> (1291), the Templars, along with other Christians in Asia, had made several attempts to regain a foothold in Syria. In 1300, we see them still fighting alongside an army of Tartars <note>Original: "Tartares." This refers to the Mongol Ilkhanate, who at the time were seen as potential allies for the Christians against the Mamluk Sultanate.</note> against the Saracens <term>Saracens: A broad term used by medieval Europeans to refer to Muslim Arabs and Turks.</term>. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

->Remarks on this new idea.<-

This conjecture is bold and unprecedented, I admit; I know everything that will be held against it. The accusation against the Templars <note>The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, a wealthy and powerful Catholic military order during the Crusades.</note> focuses solely on religion and morals. Those who have attempted to uncover their secret have all sought it within the realm of religious opinions. To claim today that it lies in ambition and politics is to contradict both their adversaries and their defenders <note>original: "apologistes"</note> simultaneously; thus, I shall refrain from claiming the honor or taking the risks of such a paradox.

Whoever wishes to support this theory will lack neither answers to objections nor plausible arguments in its favor. As for myself, I offer it only as one more combination that reinforces the hypothesis of a secret within the Order <term>Secret of the Order: The historically debated notion that the Templars possessed hidden knowledge or a private agenda revealed only to high-ranking initiates.</term>. And if, in this sense, it still seems reckless, perhaps it will be forgiven for the sake of the clarifications it has provided—clarifications which, I believe, were previously missing from this point in history. Theoretical systems serve science, provided they connect facts without distorting them.

This one, moreover, has the advantage that one can

reconcile it with any other system. The sublime historian of the *Manners of Nations* <note>original: "Mœurs des Nations"; a reference to Voltaire’s 1756 work, *Essay on the Manners and Spirit of Nations*, which was a landmark in Enlightenment historiography.</note> said a profound word: "In a heresy, one must distinguish two things: the opinion and the faction."
It is possible that among the Templars there was a secret opinion and a faction more secret still: the mystery of ambition may have hidden behind the mystery of heterodoxy <term>heterodoxy: religious beliefs or doctrines that differ from the official, established teachings of the Church.</term>. One would only be required to prove the former <note>Referring to the "faction" or political ambition.</note> as long as the latter <note>The "opinion" or religious heresy.</note> had been established with perfect solidity. We are still far from that. I can therefore, without inconsistency, rejoin the supporters of the common hypothesis and continue my research in their wake.

## CHAPTER XXV.

### Prejudice which persists against the Templars.

The secrecy of the initiations among the Templars was brought forward as a grievance against them. If it were not a grievance, it was at least a legitimate cause for prejudice. Their most skillful defender, Mr. Münter <note>Friedrich Münter (1761–1830) was a Danish scholar and bishop who wrote influential works on the history and statutes of the Knights Templar.</note>, admits as much. He observes that the statutes bear everywhere the mark of mystery, and the duties of the most rigorous discretion. He agrees that, in this regard, they far exceed the regulations of any other Order. Yet he has not said everything. He omits essential circumstances: for example, that the initiations were often, and the general chapters <term>general chapters: the supreme administrative and legislative assemblies of the Order</term> were always, not only secret, but held at night. In this regard, a curious passage by Matthew Paris <note>original: "Mathieu Pâris"; a famous 13th-century English monk and chronicler whose works are primary sources for medieval history.</note> confirms the articles of the accusation. Finally, the extraordinary precautions which, according to the depositions <note>the formal legal testimonies recorded during the trials of the Templars between 1307 and 1312</note>, were taken to isolate the assemblies and render them inaccessible and impenetrable to all eyes, are no longer in doubt, since they are found to be in agreement with this excessive mystery. # CHAPTER XXVII.

## *On the Supposed Analogy between the Trial of the Templars and those of the Heretics of the South.*

Let us come to the first and most important head of accusation, the one confessed by the vast majority of the knights, and above all, the one that was acknowledged four times and without coercion by the high officers <note>original: "grands officiers"; refers to the Order's top leadership, including the Grand Master</note> of the Order: the obligation imposed upon <term>recruits: those undergoing the initiation ceremony</term>, to deny Jesus Christ or even God, and to spit upon the cross or trample it underfoot. When one argues for the absolute injustice of the trial, this fact must either be explained or denied. ## C H A P T E R  X X V I I I.

### The Analogy is only partial.

Certain minds, says a great philosopher (1), are more inclined to notice the similarities between objects, and others to untangle their differences: the former is the mark of genius; the latter is the quality of judgment. But, according to another great man (2), false similarities are the reef upon which human reason has most often been shipwrecked. If I am mistaken in applying this last thought to the ingenious <term>apologist: someone who writes or speaks in defense of a cause, in this case Friedrich Münter defending the Knights Templar</term> discussed here, at the very least he will not complain about being recognized in the first.

The identity he believes he sees is far from appearing in the legal proceedings as clearly as it does in his curious <term>Dissertation: referring to Friedrich Münter's scholarly work on the trial of the Templars</term>. No matter how much he tries to equate the <term>Albigensians: a heretical sect in medieval southern France, also known as Cathars, who were the target of the Albigensian Crusade</term> and the <term>Templars: the powerful military order of the Crusades accused of heresy and dissolved by the Pope in 1312</term>; they are, in fact, two very different cases. Of the six categories of accusation he discusses, the second—and one of those on which he dwells the most—is the worship of the Devil and—

(1) Bacon. <note>Francis Bacon (1561–1626), the English philosopher who noted that some minds are better at seeing resemblances and others at seeing differences.</note>
(2) Plato. <note>The ancient Greek philosopher.</note>

## CHAPTER XXX.

### *Regarding the New Explanation of the Head.*

The Pope’s commissioners <note>These were officials appointed by Pope Clement V to lead the inquiry into the Order between 1309 and 1311.</note>, following testimony concerning the idol <note>The "Idol" refers to the mysterious head, sometimes called Baphomet, which the Templars were accused of worshipping in secret ceremonies.</note>, ordered a search of the Paris Temple; a relic was found there. Among these three hypotheses refuted by the Danish man of letters <note>This likely refers to Friedrich Münter (1761–1830), a Danish scholar and bishop who wrote a significant history of the Templars and investigated their alleged secret statutes.</note>, I am far from adopting any of them; they may be equally false.
