The universal history of the human spirit, that of religious cults, of superstitions, of manners and customs, and finally the history of languages—all respond unanimously to such slight difficulties. Across the entire face of the globe, one sees nations and sects practicing ceremonies of which they are ignorant of the origin, without ever thinking to seek it out. It appears certain that the consecration of physical and astronomical phenomena was everywhere the prototype for religious festivals and ceremonies. Because we cannot authentically establish the itinerary of the routes by which these practices reached us, because they have often changed along the way, and because the world is too ancient while historical monuments are too modern, must we dispute the result that presents itself before our eyes?

He knows that it was for this very reason that the fathers of the Council of the Lateran (1215) <note>The Fourth Lateran Council, one of the most important assemblies in Church history, which defined key doctrines and targeted heretical groups like the Cathars.</note> decided to burn the books of this great philosopher. The court of Rome itself, though so rigorous against simple heterodoxy <note>Beliefs or doctrines that deviate from official Church teaching.</note>, subsequently openly protected the philosophy of Averroës <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian Muslim philosopher famous for his commentaries on Aristotle. His work sparked "Latin Averroism," which sometimes argued that philosophical truth might contradict religious truth.</note>, which was a kind of atheism. This same Clement V <note>The Pope (reigned 1305–1314) who, under pressure from King Philip IV of France, suppressed the Knights Templar and oversaw their trials.</note>, who allowed the Templars to be burned, refused to have the commentary of this Arab scholar on Aristotle burned. Averroism dominated until the sixteenth century. Such is the consistency of theologians!

Thus, there is no difficulty regarding the sources from which the Templars might have derived their occult belief, their idol <note>Original: "simulacre." This likely refers to the "Baphomet," the mysterious head or image the Templars were accused of worshipping during their trials.</note>, the Greek name given to it in some places, and the Arabic name with which it was addressed. This whole bizarre tradition could have come to them from the East or the West, from the Greeks or the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval Europeans to refer to Muslims or Arabs.</note>, firsthand, tenth-hand, or hundredth-hand. Let us conclude nothing from this for or against the explanations of the fact, and even less against the credibility of the fact itself.

## *Remark on the Baphomet.*

I would be very tempted to dwell on this *Baphometus* <note>The "Baphomet," an idol or symbol the Templars were accused of worshipping. Furthermore, it is not only by its Greek quality, but also by its meaning that it announces a source of heterodoxy <note>Religious beliefs that differ from the official "orthodox" teachings of the Church.</note> other than that of the heretics from the south of France.

*BAPHÉ MÊTOUS* <note>The author is proposing a Greek etymology: "Baphe" (immersion or baptism) and "Metis" (wisdom or mind).</note>, *inspiration of the mind* <note>original Latin: "inspiratio mentis"</note>, illumination. ## CHAPTER XXXIV.

### Conclusions we must reach.

Regarding this adoration of the idol, it is better to resolve the matter with a final reflection.

It is well known that this [adoration] was never confessed by the Grand Master <note>The author refers here to Jacques de Molay (c. 1240–1314), the last Grand Master of the Knights Templar, who was burned at the stake after recanting his forced confession.</note>, nor by two of the three high-ranking officials whom the Pope, like the Grand Master himself, had reserved the right to judge personally. I further observe that among the ordinary knights, barely half acknowledged it. Could it be that the inquisitors <term>inquisitors: ecclesiastical judges tasked with the discovery and suppression of heresy</term> placed less importance on it than is generally assumed? Their objective was to destroy the Order through the charge of heresy. To convict the Order in its entirety by securing the conviction of a majority of its members was to fulfill this goal. I am therefore inclined to believe that they did not consider the idol to be an essential article of the charges. It seems to me that we should have followed their lead—insisting less on this secondary detail—and focused instead on the primary article: the great aberration of faith, the formal abjuration of Christianity, the renunciation of Jesus, and the insults directed at the sacred sign of redemption <note>This refers to the widely reported allegation that new recruits were forced to spit upon the cross during their initiation ceremony.</note>.

## CHAPTER XXXV.

### *Continuation of findings.*

There had thus formed within the heart of the Order of the Templars a sect that had its partisans and secret supporters, in greater or lesser numbers, who propagated their ideas with varying degrees of activity. This is by no means a phenomenon unique to this institution, nor is it anything strange given the customs of that time. Examples of this have been seen in several of these monastic corporations. The bizarre schism <term>schism: a formal split within a religious body</term> that divided the **Cordeliers**, and the curious history of the **Fratricelli**, are proof of this (1).

(1) The **Cordeliers** <term>Cordeliers: the name given in France to the Franciscan friars, referring to the knotted rope cord they wore as a belt</term> argued over the question of whether the bread they ate belonged to them as their own property. The **Fratricelli** <term>Fratricelli: "Little Brothers," a radical group of Franciscans who pushed for extreme poverty and were eventually condemned by the Church</term> maintained that Jesus Christ had possessed nothing; they carried the precepts of **evangelical poverty** <term>evangelical poverty: the religious ideal of living entirely without personal possessions, following the example of Jesus</term> to an extreme. These controversies—extravagant and ridiculous in their forms—concealed a very serious foundation; they attacked the wealth of the clergy and the **temporal power** <term>temporal power: the political and worldly authority of the Pope and the Church, distinct from their spiritual role</term> of the popes. The interested parties were not mistaken about this; but most of the sectaries fanatically followed impulses whose true motives were unknown to them.

# C H A P T E R XXXVI.

### *On the Authorization of Crimes against Nature.*

But such is, perhaps, the fate of all these mysterious societies, that although founded upon the purest visions of wisdom, the troublemakers and the madmen who slip into them succeed in distorting them, and infect them with abuses most opposed to their principles.

This reflection receives new evidence from the subject that remains for me to address.

The issue at hand is not a simple accusation of sodomy <term>sodomy: a historical term used in legal and religious contexts to refer to non-procreative sexual acts, specifically male-male sexual activity</term> (it is agreed upon, even by the apologists of the Templars, that if not the Order itself, at least individuals might have deserved the charge), but rather the official permission to indulge in it, which was allegedly given by the leaders to the brothers, and to the initiate <term>initiate: French: *récipiendaire*, a person being formally admitted into an order or society</term> by the superior who received him. There has been much outcry over this fact. It is rejected as a disgusting, absurd, and improbable calumny <note>calumny: a false and malicious statement designed to damage someone's reputation</note>, incompatible with the gravity of the institution and the dignity of its members. This method of refutation is more oratorical than solid. It is to judge the institution by its rules, and the individuals by their titles,

Under a burning sky, how can one remedy the heat of temperaments? Indomitable Nature delights in defying the laws that violate its own. People of the world, who have so many means to distract their senses or satisfy them, only imperfectly conceive of the excess of these passions among forced celibates in the course of a monotonous and solitary life. Inhabitants of temperate climates poorly appreciate the influence of hot countries. Do you wish to feel these contrasts? Thus were the first Christians divided; thus did later the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century which often practiced internal secrecy.</note> and so many others who recognized followers of various orders, the *perfect* <note>original: "parfaits" – a term for those who reached the highest level of initiation in certain sects.</note> and *simple believers*. If one seeks the origin of the Rosicrucians in the very elements of the name itself, one sees that the rose and the cross were alchemical <term>alchymiques: relating to alchemy, the ancient practice of seeking to transform base metals into gold and discover universal cures</term> symbols; and, as these associates were for a long time occupied almost exclusively with the philosopher’s stone <term>pierre philosophale: a legendary substance believed to facilitate the transmutation of metals and grant eternal life</term>, the purpose of this naming has nothing mysterious about it. It is well known that Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the influential French philosopher and scientist.</note>, who traveled all over Germany from 1620 to 1625 to discover them, was unable to find them there.

Yet, regardless, it has been observed that Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the central figure of the Protestant Reformation, whose "Luther Rose" seal featured a cross at the center of a rose.</note> had adopted these same attributes of the rose and the cross for his seal from the beginning of the sixteenth century.

# CHAPTER XXXIX.

## *Epilogue.*

In concluding these reflections and these studies, I will respond in advance to the criticisms that might be directed at them.

Among men of intellect, there are too many who treat even the most serious readings as mere entertainment, for whom truth is only a secondary benefit, if indeed it is not a matter of complete indifference to them. These individuals would like to find in every kind of work the merit of a good play—the appeal of an engaging plot and a satisfying conclusion <note>In historical writing, a "satisfying conclusion" usually refers to a clear-cut verdict of guilt or innocence, which the author is avoiding.</note>. These people, perhaps, will resent me for not having enlisted among the opponents or among the <term>apologists</term> <note>Apologists: individuals who write or speak in defense of a particular cause, person, or organization—in this case, those defending the Knights Templar against the historical charges of heresy.</note> of the Templars. They will condemn this sort of <term>skepticism</term> <note>Skepticism: here, the author refers to the practice of doubting or suspending judgment when the evidence is not conclusive.</note> in which I find myself wavering despite my best efforts. They will not like to see me testing one <term>hypothesis</term> <note>Hypothesis: a proposed explanation based on limited evidence, used as a starting point for further investigation.</note> after another without recommending one to them in preference to another. But it is not my fault if experience teaches me that the fundamental nature of things is, in every field, nearly impenetrable. Why do I find in—

As it was undeniably a difficult undertaking, especially since the <term>grand-maître</term> <note>Jacques de Molay, the supreme head of the Knights Templar.</note> had only a single serving brother <note>A non-noble member of the Order who performed administrative or domestic duties; here, his only available companion for advice.</note> with him with whom he could deliberate, the <term>commissioners</term> <note>The group of high-ranking clergy appointed by the Pope to investigate the Order.</note> advised him to reflect maturely on what he was committing to, and particularly to consider his own confession against <term>the Order</term> and against himself. But if, for reasonable motives, he believed he should persist in his design, they were for their part ready to accept him for the *defense*, even to grant him time for reflection if he requested it: he should only know that in matters of faith and <term>heresy</term>, a simple procedure is followed, and that the usual delays in trials and the trickery of lawyers can in no way take place.

To better enable him to reflect maturely, the <term>commissioners</term> as a precaution, in his presence, had the <term>apostolic bull</term> <note>A formal public decree issued by the Pope, named for the "bulla" or lead seal used to authenticate it.</note> read and explained in the <term>common tongue</term> <note>The "langue vulgaire" or vernacular (French), which was the language spoken by the knights, as they often did not understand the official Latin of the Church.</note>; this was the document by which the inquiry against <term>the Order</term> was delegated to them, along with four other <term>papal briefs</term> <note>Shorter, less formal administrative letters from the Pope.</note> related to it, including their own citation of <term>the Order</term>. Also, that a greater error prevails, and has prevailed, which they hold and have held in times past: that the Grand Master himself can absolve the brothers of the Order from sins, even those not confessed, which they omitted to confess out of some shame or fear of the penance that might be enjoined or inflicted <note>original: "pœnitentiæ injungendæ vel infligendæ"; in medieval canon law, only a priest had the power to absolve sins. The charge that the Grand Master (usually a layman) performed this rite was a serious accusation of heresy</note>.

109. Also, that the Grand Master confessed these aforementioned errors before his arrest, voluntarily, in the presence of trustworthy clerics and laymen.

110. Also, that [he did so] in the presence of the senior commanders <term>præceptoribus<gloss>High-ranking officers who managed the Order's various estates and provinces</gloss></term> of his Order.

111. Also, that they hold and have held the aforementioned errors, not only believing and holding these things regarding the Grand Master, but also regarding the other commanders and leaders of the Order, especially the visitors <term>visitatoribus<gloss>Officials appointed to inspect the different houses of the Order to ensure discipline and financial order</gloss></term>.

112. Also, that whatever the Grand Master did, ordained, or established—especially in conjunction with his convent <note>original: "conventu suo"; the central high council or headquarters of the Order</note>—the entire Order was bound to hold and observe, and indeed did observe.

113. Also, that this power belonged to him and had resided in him from of old.

114. Also, that the aforementioned wicked ways and errors lasted for so long that the membership of the Order could have been renewed once, twice, or many times during the period these errors were introduced or observed.

115. Also, that all, or nearly two-thirds of the Order, knowing of the said errors, neglected to correct them.

<summary>This page details the legal charges against the Templars concerning the Grand Master's unauthorized power to absolve sins and the absolute authority he held over the Order. It argues that these "errors" were long-standing, known by the majority of members, and confessed to by the Grand Master himself.</summary>
<keywords>Grand Master, absolution of sins, confession, heresy, Commanders, Visitors, Convent, trial of the Templars, institutional corruption</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the formal articles of accusation against the Order of the Temple, specifically articles 116 through 125. The previous page discussed the Order’s internal belief that their leaders could grant absolution for sins—a power usually reserved for priests—and how the Grand Master had already confessed to these "errors." This page moves to the public consequences of these practices: the failure to report them to the Church, the resulting public scandal among the kings of Europe, and the confessions made by high-ranking officials of the Order.</meta>

<page-num>343</page-num>
<header>on the Templars.</header>

116. *Likewise, that they neglected to report [these matters] to the Holy Mother Church.*

117. *Likewise, that they did not withdraw from the practice of the aforementioned errors or from the communion of the said brothers, even though they had the opportunity to leave and to do what was right.*

118. *Likewise, that many brothers of the said Order left because of the filth <note>original: "fœditates"; this term was used by the inquisitors to imply moral and physical corruption, often specifically referencing the charges of ritual sodomy or blasphemy</note> and errors of the same Order, some transferring to another religious order and some returning to secular life.*

119. *Likewise, that because of each and every one of the aforementioned points, great scandals have arisen against the said Order, stirred in the hearts of high-ranking persons—even kings and princes—and of almost the entire Christian population.*

120. *Likewise, that all and each of the aforementioned things are well-known and manifest among the brothers of the said Order.*

121. *Likewise, that concerning these matters there is a public outcry, common opinion, and general notoriety <note>original: "fama"; in medieval law, "publica fama" or public report was a legal requirement to initiate an official inquiry into a crime</note> both among the brothers of the said Order and outside of it.*

122. *Likewise, regarding the greater part of the aforementioned charges.*

123. *Likewise, regarding some of them.*

124. *Likewise, that the Grand Master of the Order, the Visitor <term>visitator<gloss>An inspector general responsible for auditing the Order's houses and maintaining discipline across a wide region</gloss></term>, and the Grand Preceptor <term>magnus præceptor<gloss>A high-ranking regional commander; in this context, those overseeing the key provinces of the Order</gloss></term> of Cyprus, Normandy, and Poitou <note>original: "Cypri, Normaniæ, Pictaviæ"</note>, and many other preceptors and several other brothers of the said Order, confessed to the premises both in court and out of court, before solemn persons, and in several places before public officials.*

125. *Likewise, that several brothers of the said Order, both knights <term>milites<gloss>The elite noble fighters of the Order who took monastic vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience</gloss></term> and priests <term>sacerdotes<gloss>The ordained clergy who lived within the Order to provide sacraments and spiritual guidance to the knights</gloss></term>, and others in the presence of the Lord*

<summary>This page outlines the legal charges regarding the public scandal caused by the Templars' alleged "errors" and notes that many high-ranking officials, including regional commanders of Cyprus and Normandy, had already confessed to these crimes. It emphasizes that the Order's reputation was ruined not only among the common people but also among the kings and princes of Christendom.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the formal articles of accusation (the "rubrics") against the Order of the Temple. It follows the previous page’s discussion of the public scandal and the "notoriety" of the Order's alleged crimes. It then transitions from the legal charges to a narrative account of the trial proceedings in Paris in March 1310, specifically the attempt by the rank-and-file brothers to organize a collective defense.</meta>

<page-num>344</page-num>
<header>Historical Memoirs</header>

*...[before] our pope and the lord cardinals, they confessed the aforementioned things or a large part of the said errors.* <note>original: "nostri papæ et dominorum cardinalium fuerunt prædicta vel magnam partem dictorum errorum confessi"</note>
126. *Likewise, that [these things were confirmed] by oaths sworn by the same men.* <note>original: "per juramenta præstita ab eisdem"</note>
127. *Likewise, that they acknowledged the aforementioned things even in a full consistory.* <note>original: "in pleno consistorio recognoverunt prædicta"; a consistory is a formal meeting of the Pope and his college of cardinals, representing the highest level of ecclesiastical testimony.</note>

**On the 28th**, the brothers who had offered themselves as defenders of their Order were gathered on a lawn behind the episcopal residence. The commission <note>the group of bishops and officials appointed by the Pope to investigate the Order</note> informed them that it would accept their proxies <note>legal representatives or attorneys</note> for this defense, whom they could elect up to the number of ten or even more, and who would have the freedom to communicate with them. The brothers deliberated among themselves. Speaking through Raynal de Pruin and Pierre de Boulogne <note>two prominent Templars who led the legal defense; Pierre de Boulogne was a priest and the Order's procurator at the papal court</note>, they complained of ill-treatment and excused themselves from naming legal representatives without the consent of their superiors. The commissioners replied that the Grand Master <note>Jacques de Molay</note>, the Visitor of France <note>Hugues de Pairaud</note>, and several Grand Priors had their reasons for not taking up the defense of the Order themselves. They strongly urged the brothers to name their representatives.

The list of brothers gathered that day before the commissioners numbered 544 (1).

---

(1) The list that follows has never been published, and no other historical record <note>original: "monument"; in this context, a historical document or piece of evidence</note> makes known such a large number of Templars.

The commission decided that two of the notaries who served as its clerks would travel to the various locations where these brothers were being held, accompanied by the four who had spoken on their behalf, to assure them all that the <term>procurators|Legal representatives or attorneys authorized to act on behalf of others in a court of law</term> they named would be accepted.

This visit, which occupied the first days of August, was unsuccessful. Several brothers, such as **Praine** (1), **Boulogne**, and others, submitted articles of justification. These can be found in the works of Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651) was a French scholar who compiled a famous collection of documents regarding the trial of the Templars.</note>, and several other historians have reported them. However, almost all of them generally refused to name procurators for various reasons, the main ones being:

1. Without our leaders <note>Refers to the Grand Master and other high-ranking officials of the Order.</note>, we cannot name representatives.
2. Each of us will defend himself individually.
3. That we be reunited with our brothers.
4. That specific individuals be allowed to travel through the prisons to consult with the others.
5. That the leaders be placed in the hands of the Church <note>original: "l’Eglise". The brothers likely preferred the jurisdiction of the Pope over that of the King's inquisitors.</note>.

(1) Or *Pruin*; in Latin *of Provins* <note>original Latin: "de Pruino". Provins was a major center for the Templars in France.</note>.

On April 7, these same four Templars—**Robert de Pruine** <note>Also known in other records as Raynald or Renaud de Pruino, a primary legal defender for the Order.</note>, **Pierre de Boulogne** <note>The Order's procurator-general at the papal court.</note>, **Chambonnet**, and **Sartiges**—presented, on behalf of all the others, the known articles of defense. These began with the phrases *Before you* <note>original: "Coram vobis"</note> and *That the procurators* <note>original: "Quod procuratores"</note>, etc. **Jean de Montroyal** added his own proposals to these on behalf of his fellow prisoners, which Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651), a French scholar who published the primary documents of the trial.</note> has provided in the Catalan language. The commissioners rejected some of their assertions. (*See* Dupuy.)

A passage from this petition indicates that torture and <term>hardships|The original "gênes" refers to both physical constraints and specific instruments of torture</term> were still continuing in the prisons.

On April 11, the commissioners summoned the four brothers who had appeared on behalf of the others for the defense of the Order to witness the swearing-in of the witnesses to be heard. The intent was for them to witness the spirit of justice in which the proceedings would be conducted; however, there was no intention of recognizing them as official <term>defenders of the Order|Legal counsel with full standing in the court</term>, as opposing parties, or as agents of the investigation. The four brothers reserved the right to speak regarding the character and the depositions of the witnesses.

**1st witness.** — *Raoul de Presles*, <term>jurisconsult|A legal expert or jurist</term>.

### on the Templars.

(His deposition is reported by Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651) was a French scholar who compiled primary documents regarding the trial of the Templars.</note>). He held from a knight of the Temple that there was a very secret point of the Order, as well as a highly hidden book of statutes. This knight had, through his mediation, obtained entry to the <term>general chapter|The supreme assembly of the Order's leaders</term>. He had also spoken to him of the terrible prisons which, within the Order, were used to punish disobedience.

2nd witness. — *Nicolas Simon*, provost of Saint-Maur, testified to similar things, and regarding the same knight.

3rd witness. — *Jean de Saint-Benoît*, prior of l’Isle-Bouchard, diocese of Tours, received into the Order 40 years ago. He was ill, even at the point of death. Three of the commissioners, accompanied by notaries, were sent to him to hear his testimony. He confessed to the renunciation of Jesus Christ and spitting on the cross; however, he implicated only himself <note>The phrase "il ne charge que lui seul" suggests he took personal responsibility for these acts rather than accusing the entire Order of institutionalizing them.</note>.

4th witness. — *Guischard de Marziac*, a secular knight <note>A knight who was not a member of a religious or military order like the Templars.</note>, aged 50. He cited many places in France, Italy, and Spain where he had heard the crimes listed in the first articles attributed to the Order. In Toulouse, he had arranged for a man named Hugues de Marchand to be received into the Order. After he had dubbed him a knight, the brothers led him away and held him

Marziac took him aside the next day and wanted to know the cause of this distress that was still visible on his face. Marchand replied that it was impossible <note>Meaning it was impossible to speak of what had occurred due to the oath of secrecy.</note>, and that he would never be happy again for the rest of his life; indeed, Marziac had always seen him sad from that time onward. He answers in detail, following the questions of the commissioners, but remains rather vague on certain points.

# on the Templars.

On the 23rd, the four Boulogne brothers, etc., present a new petition. (See in Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651) was a French scholar who published a seminal collection of documents regarding the trial of the Templars.</note> the article <note>original Latin: "completa vero et perfecta.... coram vobis.... quod processus habitus contra ipsos...."</note> "complete indeed and perfect... before you... that the proceedings held against them..." setting out the means of violence and enticement used to extract the confessions of those who testified against the Order, asking that certain precautions be taken against the witnesses, etc., and finally requesting a hearing for brother Valincourt. He had left the Order to enter a more severe profession, that of the **Carthusians** <note>A monastic order known for its extreme austerity, silence, and solitude.</note>. But since then, he desired to return to the Temple and submitted himself to a rigorous penance to obtain this—something a man like him would not have done for a perverted society.

### April 24.

7th witness. — *Buris* confesses to most of the points; spitting on the cross, renunciation of Jesus, and obscene kisses; the head or the idol, which he describes as a human figure with a long beard; he reports the formula in these words: *I deny God*, but denies that there is an anti-Christian doctrine, and knows nothing of the permission for impure relations <note>A euphemism for the accusations of sodomy leveled against the Order.</note> between the brothers.

### April 27 and 28.

8th witness. — *Gérard de Passage*. Here is what he says of his initiation, which had taken place in Nicosia in the East <note>Nicosia is the capital of Cyprus; at this time, it was a central hub for the Templars after the fall of Acre in 1291.</note>. 
> "I was presented with a wooden crucifix: I was asked if I believed that this was the Lord God? I said it was the image of Jesus crucified. Do not believe that (was the response), *it is nothing more than a piece of wood. Our Lord is in Heaven....*"
Ordered to spit upon and trample the crucifix underfoot, he obeyed; then came the obscene kisses <note>A standard accusation in the trial, involving ritualistic kisses on the lower back, navel, or mouth during initiation.</note> at the base of the back; but not on bare skin. In the span of sixteen years, he had lived in seven houses <note>A "house" refers to a Templar commandery or local headquarters.</note>, both in the East and in Europe. Since the Templars had been arrested, he had escaped twice and had been horribly tortured at Mâcon, by the order of the officer who commanded there for the king. The cord <note>Templars wore a small cord or girdle over their shirts as a symbol of chastity. The prosecution alleged these were used in magical rites involving idols.</note> mentioned in the articles as a magical ceremony was nothing but a symbol indicating that any knight taken prisoner by the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims, particularly those fighting against the Crusaders.</note> would have no other ransom <note>This likely refers to the Templar rule that a brother could not be ransomed with money, only with his belt or a knife, implying they must be prepared for martyrdom.</note>. He had heard talk of the corruption of the Order for twenty years.

9th witness. — *Geoffroi Thatan*, confesses the first four articles <note>These "articles" typically included the denial of Christ, spitting on the cross, obscene kisses, and the encouragement of sodomy.</note>; had been received by the

He also recounts being tortured at Mâcon following his escape from arrest.</summary>

On May 10, the four brother-defenders appeared, with Pierre de Boulogne acting as their spokesperson.

The Archbishop of Sens, along with his suffragans <term>suffragans: Bishops who are subordinate to an archbishop within a specific ecclesiastical province.</term>, in their provincial council convened in Paris, was due the following day to pass final judgment on many brothers who had committed themselves to the defense of the Order. This was clearly an attempt to force the others to abandon any plan of defense; in response to this, they had drawn up an appeal which they wished to submit to the commissioners. The latter declared that they could not formally receive it, but could only hear it read aloud.

There follows this act reported by Dupuy <note>Pierre Dupuy (1582–1651) was a French historian and librarian who published a major collection of documents concerning the trial of the Templars.</note>:
> “Before you, etc. That they fear, based on probable conjectures, etc.” <note>original Latin: "coram vobis, etc. Quod ex verisimilibus conjecturis timent, etc." This refers to the legal argument that the defenders feared for their lives or the fairness of the trial based on the actions of the provincial council.</note> *See Dupuy*.

The commissioners decided to take this incident into consideration. The defenders submitted a new petition. That very evening, the commissioners promised the defenders that they would hold a conference with the bishops of the council and do everything they believed possible.

14th witness. — ***Humbert de Puy***, a serving brother <term>serving brother: A non-noble member of the Order, often performing manual or supportive tasks rather than military service.</term>, tortured three times: he said he had not denied [his faith]; but he confessed to having heard it spoken of.

15th witness. — ***Bortaldi***, a serving brother: he confesses to the four articles <note>These "four articles" refer to the primary charges leveled against the Order: the denial of Christ, spitting on the cross, the "obscene kiss" during initiation, and the practice of sodomy.</note>.

On May 12, during this same interrogation, the commissioners were informed that on this very day, fifty-four Templars, who had committed themselves to the defense of the Order before them, were to be burned at the stake. They sent word to the Archbishop of Sens and the council, inviting them to reflect upon this plan and to delay the execution, especially since the brothers who had recently died in prison had, with their final breath, sworn upon their salvation to their own innocence and that of the Order. The commissioners added that if such a judgment were executed, the course of their own inquiry would be completely obstructed, since witnesses had already lost their reason out of terror at this news and appeared incapable of sustaining further interrogations.

**35<sup>th</sup> witness.** — Tilley, a serving brother, 70 years old, recounts his reception with circumstances that resemble those of Freemasonry. <note>The author here draws a parallel between the Templar initiation and 18th-century Masonic rites, a common comparison made by historians of this period to explain the ritualized secrecy.</note> There were repeated urgings for admission. — Exhortations to reflect; warnings about hardships, privations, and dangers. — Repeatedly being sent back for solitary reflection. — A call made three times. — Instructions from the receptor <term>Receptor: The high-ranking official presiding over the initiation of a new member.</term> after the reception regarding the general duties of a knight. He then reports the secret details, just as the others did. But it was not as *points of the Order* <note>original: "points d'Ordre" — refers to the official statutes or mandatory rules of the Templar Rule.</note> that these impieties and outrages had been prescribed to him. *“Are you not my subject?”* the receptor said to him. Tilley viewed all of this as tests of his submission. He remarks that the receptor had himself kissed and devoutly adored that same cross which he was making him spit upon. — 
> “On my conscience, I myself do not know what I should say of it.”
This is his final answer to the very detailed questions of the commissioners.

He is asked: “Why did you first allow yourself to be tortured, rather than confessing all of this?” — “Because I did not believe that our trial would take such a bad turn.” <note>original: "tournure" — meaning the direction or outcome of the proceedings.</note> He shows a great knowledge of the statutes <term>Statutes: The formal rules and regulations governing the daily life and legal structure of the Order of the Temple.</term>, and cites several infractions of these rules. He speaks of a reception held six months before the imprisonment at which the King <note>Referring to King Philip IV (the Fair) of France, who orchestrated the downfall of the Templars.</note> was present: it was beyond reproach. He is asked if, at that time, the trial was foreseen? — I do not know.

Regarding Article 114, he answers: none of the authors of these abuses are still alive.

Not all members, nor even all the high-ranking leaders of the Order, were informed of them.

To remedy this problem, they were organized into detachments that served as garrisons on small islands or in fortresses.

He had once been commissioned to lead a newly received member to the *secret interview* <note>original: "entretien secret." This likely refers to private instructions given to new members about the Order’s inner rules or, as the inquisitors suspected, its alleged secret heresies.</note>, but he had refused under a pretext.

### Historical Memoirs

He had seen at the Pilgrims' Castle <note>original: "château des Pelerins." A ridiculous fable regarding the head <note>The witness is dismissing the common accusation that the Templars worshipped a mysterious idol or severed head, often referred to as Baphomet.</note>. Furthermore, he knew of no such thing that was considered to properly belong to the Order.

He reports, as certain facts, the intrigues that had preceded the election of Grand Master Molay; it had taken place in the East (1).

The electors were divided. The assembly could not reach a consensus on any candidate. Those from the provinces of Limousin and Auvergne declared for Hugues de Peyraud and held the advantage. Molay’s faction was weaker. Seeing his lack of power, Molay declared before Eudes de Grandisson and other highly significant knights that he no longer laid claim to the position and would vote for Peyraud. This promise persuaded the majority to appoint him to the rank of Grand Prior <term>Grand Prior: a high-ranking officer in the Order who often governed as an interim leader upon the death of a Grand Master.</term>, whom it was customary to name to govern following the death of the Grand Master. Then Molay changed his tone, and he used his authority and influence to force the assembly to elect him Grand Master. This witness knew Latin.

(1) The year 1298.

His reception was conducted like the others; but at the moment he was being forced to renounce, and during the other points of the rule, a call to arms was sounded for an attack by the Saracens <term>Saracens: A term used by medieval Europeans to refer to Muslims, particularly those in the Holy Land during the Crusades.</term>. Those who were receiving him had only enough time to make him swear an oath of secrecy. He was told afterward that all of this had been done only as a jest and to put him to the test. In fact, he has never since heard anything similar.

228th witness. — *J. de Noyon*, confesses to the renunciation, but of himself alone.
